Foreign Minister Penny Wong, Indigenous Australians Minister Malarndirri McCarthy, her Opposition counterpart Julian Leeser, and the Northern Territory Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro all addressed the Garma forums.

But Ryan would have liked to see more open discussion and concession from politicians about the impact of racism.

"That's the fundamental issue, as we speak, that's holding back our people in terms of expanding job opportunity, business opportunity.

Thorpe is a member of the parliamentary committee that's been conducting the hearings to collect testimony from First Nations people across the country about their experience of racism.

"We need to highlight racism as a real problem for everyone in this country, not just for Aboriginal people, but for non-Aboriginal people," she said.

"Like, do you want to be proud of being in a racist country, and standing by while people are being racially vilified and harmed?

"Racism kills. Racism makes people sick. Racism is like a cancer, and if you subscribe to that, then you've got a problem, and you need to have a look at that problem in detail ... a royal commission will certainly expose that."

Thorpe had initially called for the terms of reference for the existing royal commission investigating antisemitism and social cohesion to be broadened to include racism against First Nations Australians.

"The government weren't interested. They just wanted to focus on antisemitism. There's racism against black and brown people in this country that's actually killing us."

"Our people have poured their hearts and souls out. They've been retraumatized, telling their stories again and again," she said.

summary.en: Shrijana Ghising is one of the best in the world. Now she's chasing a Paralympics dream for Australia

body.en:
Eight years later, the 26-year-old is one of the world's top athletes in the sport and is chasing a place at the 2028 Paralympic Games in Los Angeles.

And as one of Australia's newest citizens, she hopes she will be wearing green and gold.

Originally from Nepal, Ghising won silver at the Gangwon-Chuncheon 2026 World Para Taekwondo Open Challenge in South Korea earlier this month — her first international tournament representing Australia.

"I'm so excited that now I am a citizen I can represent Australia in all the tournaments, but the big goal is LA28 … I want to be a medallist representing Australia," she said.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

She travelled to Australia on holiday in 2023 but quickly fell in love with the country.

"I have experienced a lot of discrimination in my life, but when I came to Australia everyone was very kind, and they did not treat me differently because of my disability," she said.

"I love Australia, its culture and its people … I came for a holiday, but it became my home."

Ghising lived in Burnie, Tasmania, for two years before moving to Melbourne to further pursue her taekwondo career.

"My mother and my life partner motivated me to fulfil my taekwondo journey," she said.

Under special provisions of the Citizenship Act and with authorisation from Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, Ghising's citizenship application was expedited so she could compete for Australia at upcoming tournaments.

She officially became an Australian citizen at a ceremony in Melbourne's inner-west in June — just in time to represent Australia at the Para Taekwondo Open Challenge.

Australia has a special citizenship pathway for elite athletes and coaches to represent the country internationally.

The law was changed last year so Australian permanent residents who train or compete overseas as part of their sporting commitments are not disadvantaged in their pathway to citizenship, a move welcomed by the Australian Olympic Committee and Paralympics Australia.

However, refugee advocacy groups have previously said the rules should be broadened to include all people applying for Australian citizenship.

In 2009, when the government proposed shortening residency requirements for elite athletes, the Federation of Ethnic Communities' Councils of Australia welcomed the change but said it wanted everybody to be treated equally under citizenship law.

In 2024-25, a total of 165,193 people became Australian citizens, representing over 190 different nationalities.

title.en: Is your 2026 Census data private? What the ABS can and cannot share
title.zh: 您的 2026 年人口普查数据是私有的吗？ ABS 可以分享什么，不能分享什么

summary.en: Information, including names and addresses, collected during the 2026 Census must be destroyed after processing.
summary.zh: 这是一则来自澳洲栏目的新闻，重点涉及真理、分辨与诚实。如需完整细节，请阅读英文原始报道。

body.en:
On Census night, Australians will be asked to provide personal information — including their name and address — to the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).

These details remain confidential and cannot be shared with police, registered migration agents or any government department.

Jenny Telford, general manager of the Census and Population division at the ABS, said keeping people's data safe and private was "absolutely critical".

"The ABS has lots of protections, including legal protections, that mean we can never release information in any way that can identify an individual or a household," she told SBS News.

"When you complete that Census form, your name and address are kind of separated away from all of the other answers on the form really early in our process, and we also make commitments that we adhere to to destroy names and addresses once we've processed the Census and produced the statistics that ... Australia needs."

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

Since 1911, names and addresses have been collected as part of the national Census of Population and Housing.

The ABS reports collecting this information improves the "accuracy and efficiency of data linkage" and the quality of statistics.

After the Census processing period is complete, no-one working with Census data is able to view personal identifiers at the same time as survey results.

Names included in this year's Census forms will be retained for up to 18 months after the Census, until the end of February 2028. Addresses are retained for a maximum of 36 months until the end of August 2029.

People can also choose to have their information preserved for 99 years as part of the Census Time Capsule. This information is securely transferred to the National Archives of Australia, the agency responsible for collecting and preserving government documents.

Personal information cannot be accessed for any reason until 2125. If a person elects to transfer their information to the archives, this decision cannot be reversed, according to the ABS.

All ABS staff, including temporary employees, are legally bound to never release information collected during the Census. This includes staff past or present.

Penalties for sharing information collected during the Census (whether directly or indirectly) include fines of up to $26,400 and up to two years' imprisonment.

title.en: You won't believe what we've left in space. It could be nearing a 'tipping point'
title.zh: 你不会相信我们在太空中留下了什么。它可能接近“临界点”

summary.en: Humans have left an extraordinary amount of stuff beyond Earth. What does the SpaceX moon crash tell us about what's to come?
summary.zh: 这是一则来自澳洲栏目的新闻，重点涉及智慧、知识与追求真理。如需完整细节，请阅读英文原始报道。

body.en:
Experts fear space is becoming dangerously crowded, as a new era of exploration sends ever more objects into orbit and to the moon.

The recent crash of a huge chunk of SpaceX rocket debris into the moon has renewed attention on the surprisingly large collection of human-made material in space.

From golf balls, bags of excrement and flags on the lunar surface to rocket wreckage, abandoned tools and countless pieces of debris orbiting Earth, astronomers warn that there are consequences to treating space as a dumping ground.

The bus-sized 4000kg hunk of SpaceX debris came from a Falcon 9 rocket that launched a US and a Japanese lunar lander toward the moon in January last year.

Although no direct image of the impact has emerged, astronomers detected a plume of debris consistent with the rocket crashing into the lunar surface.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

Just months ago, four NASA astronauts flew to the moon and back for the first time in more than 50 years. With the second race to the moon well underway — and the United States aiming to establish a base on the lunar surface — the recent SpaceX impact has renewed questions about whether humans are repeating old mistakes off-planet.

Experts say the number of objects orbiting Earth, meanwhile, is increasing the risk of collisions — and without intervention, could make some orbits too dangerous to use.

It's estimated the lunar surface now holds nearly 200 tonnes of human-made material across about 3,000 objects accumulated since the Soviet Union's Luna 2 became the first spacecraft to reach the Moon in 1959.

According to a NASA catalogue, items on the moon include everything from a gold olive branch left behind by Neil Armstrong in 1969, to earplugs, urine collection devices, a hammer, moon boots, cameras, a javelin and two golf balls.

"There are fairly small things all over the moon," associate professor Ben Montet, an astronomy researcher at the University of New South Wales, told SBS News.

"Remnants of the Apollo missions are still there. The lunar lander is there, and the rovers that came with the later missions, but also the silly things like the golf ball that the astronaut on the last mission hit. That's still out there somewhere."

Materials from other moon missions, including robotic probes landed by the former Soviet Union and other nations, also remain scattered across the surface.

Scientists were not particularly concerned about the recent SpaceX collision with the moon's surface, and a NASA spokesperson said it posed no danger to Earth.

title.en: What the upcoming nationwide e-bike crackdown means for you
title.zh: 即将到来的全国电动自行车整治对您意味着什么

summary.en: New regulations are currently being developed for the sale of electric bikes, scooters, and skateboards across Australia.
summary.zh: 澳大利亚正在起草电动自行车、滑板车和滑板销售的新标准。

body.en:
A nationwide crackdown on high-speed e-bikes will seek to close regulatory loopholes after years of rising accidents and injuries, the federal government has announced.

On Thursday, Labor instructed the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) to draft new standards for the sale of "e-micromobility" devices.

The new standards will apply to electric bikes, scooters and skateboards and are designed to prevent the sale of high-risk devices following a spike in e-bike injuries.

Assistant Competition Minister Andrew Leigh said the changes would inspire confidence in Australian consumers and send a clear message to industry.

"Nationally consistent standards will provide clearer expectations for manufacturers, retailers and consumers alike," he said.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

Currently, regulatory enforcement varies between states and territories. Retailers can exploit the resultant loopholes to sell non-compliant devices.

Last year, Australia's state transport ministers agreed to mandate the international EN 15194 standard as the primary benchmark for e-bikes.

These standards restrict e-bikes to operating primarily through pedal assistance, cap their output, and require them to cut power once they reach 25km/h.

The new rules drafted by the ACCC will aim to close existing gaps after years of concerns over injuries and accidents, including from high-powered e-bikes.

The new consumer standards were proposed at a meeting of federal, state and territory consumer affairs ministers in Darwin in July.

Harold Scruby, chief executive at the Pedestrian Council of Australia, said the announcement was a welcome step forward, but long overdue.

Any changes must be complemented by consequences for retailers who fail to meet compliance standards, Scruby said.

"We've really got to clamp down on these cowboys who are selling these things to young children," he said.

Asked whether the horse had already bolted, Leigh insisted the changes complemented state-level crackdowns.

"There's work underway through transport ministers," he told Seven's Sunrise program on Thursday.

E-bikes have been spruiked as an environmentally friendly, cost-affordable answer to congested city streets.

But the rollout of shared e-bike schemes — like Lime bikes and others — as well as their broader uptake across the nation have been clouded by rising injury and accident rates.

In 2024, NSW recorded 226 injuries related to e-bikes, which surged to 233 in the first seven months of 2025, including four deaths.
